title: The "Satanic Panic" of the 1980s
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine the Satanic panic of the 1980s, a roughly decade-long American moral panic claiming widespread Satanic death cults abducting and abusing children, which they argue was fabricated. They trace historical roots (witch persecutions, blood libel, 19th-century art, 1960s-70s horror films, Mike Warren Key's 1972 book, the 1980 book Michelle Remembers), describe the child-protection and daycare context, the McMartin and Keller daycare cases, recovered memory therapy, Paul Ingram's false confession, media role (Geraldo, Oprah, Sally Jesse Raphael), the exonerations and the National Center on Child Abuse and Neglect survey that found no evidence of Satanic cults. Ends with listener mail about Children's Miracle Network balloon donations.

entities.name: National Center on Child Abuse and Neglect

segments.title: Opening and framing the Satanic panic
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode, recall growing up amid Satanic rumors, and argue the 1980s Satanic panic was a moral panic built on claims that were almost entirely made up.

segments.title: Historical roots: witch persecutions, blood libel and fiction
segments.summary: They trace ancient and medieval roots of accusations of devil worship and baby's blood, such as blood libel against Jews and Romans' accusations against Christians, and the witch persecutions. They note how repeated fiction and sensational stories gained the status of fact.

segments.title: Twentieth-century fiction, film, music and occult figures
segments.summary: The hosts discuss early 20th-century fiction, 1960s-70s horror films such as The Devil Rides Out, Rosemary's Baby, The Omen and The Exorcist, Satanic imagery in heavy metal and backmasking, and occult figures Alistair Crowley and Anton LaVey, whose theatrics fed the idea of real Satanic cults.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break before the next section.

segments.title: 1970s child abuse awareness and stranger danger
segments.summary: In the 1970s America became more aware of child abuse, leading to mandatory reporting laws and a child protection movement. Women returning to work and leaving children in daycare heightened parental anxiety, and the media sensationalized child crime stories.

segments.title: Keller daycare case and the snowball of accusations
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Keller daycare case in Austin, Texas, where the Kellers were accused of extreme abuse including killings and sharks; the case began with a three-year-old's accusation, a therapist's coaxing, and parents comparing notes. Flawed medical testimony bolstered the case.

segments.title: Recovered memory therapy and Michelle Remembers
segments.summary: The hosts explain recovered memory therapy and the 1980 book Michelle Remembers, co-written with therapist Lawrence Pazder, which popularized claims of ritual abuse. They note the book's influence, its debunking, and professional statements on repressed memory and suggestibility, including research by Elizabeth Loftus.

segments.title: Paul Ingram false confession
segments.summary: Paul Ingram, a sheriff's deputy and fundamentalist preacher, was accused by his daughter of Satanic ritual abuse and confessed despite no memory of it; he served about twenty years in prison.

segments.title: Media, talk shows and the role of experts
segments.summary: Talk shows such as Geraldo Rivera's two-hour special Exposing Satan's Underground, Sally Jesse Raphael and Oprah fueled the panic. A children's book and anatomically correct dolls were used in therapy and court, and the hosts say psychologists, media and law enforcement share blame along with self-interested Satanic experts.

segments.title: McMartin trial, exonerations and the end of the panic
segments.summary: The McMartin trial in Southern California became the longest and most expensive US trial with no convictions. An HBO film and the exoneration of Margaret Kelly Michaels helped turn the tide, and a 1990 National Center on Child Abuse and Neglect study found no evidence of Satanic cults. The West Memphis Three and Paradise Lost documentaries are discussed.
topics: National Center on Child Abuse and Neglect study

segments.title: Why people believed it: subversion ideology and rumor panic
segments.summary: The hosts review sociological explanations: subversion ideology, rumor panic, and urban legend as metaphor, plus millennial anxiety. They close the content by questioning which moral panics exist today.

segments.title: Listener mail: Children's Miracle Network balloons
segments.summary: A listener writing on behalf of Children's Miracle Network disputes the hosts' claim that buying the hospital balloons helps stores get tax credits; the hosts say they will look into it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to the website and social channels for more on the topics.
